title: Gigantes Plaki
style: Greek baked giant beans — slow-cooked in a sweet tomato and olive oil sauce until the top catches and the sauce turns jammy
description: The Greek taverna classic: giant beans simmered until properly tender, then baked slowly in tomato, onion, and a serious amount of olive oil until the sauce thickens and the top browns.

items.note: elephant beans, or large butter/lima beans — for the quick version use 3 x 400 g tins, see first tip
divided — 80 ml for the base, 30 ml with the beans, 40 ml over the top
2 tins, or ripe grated fresh tomatoes in season
only if the tomatoes are sharp
seasoned only after the beans are tender
wilted and squeezed dry — see step 5
chopped — the signature note, don't skip
optional, chopped — good with the greens version
raw, poured over at the end
optional, crumbled over — no longer vegan

steps: Soak: Cover the beans with plenty of cold water, stir in the tablespoon of salt, and leave overnight or at least 8 hours. Salted soaking water softens the skins — it does not toughen them.

Simmer: Drain, cover with fresh unsalted water, add the bay leaf, and bring to a gentle boil. Skim the foam, then simmer 60–90 minutes until a bean crushes easily against the roof of your mouth. Go by the test, not the clock — older and larger beans can take well over 90 minutes. They must be fully tender now. Drain, keeping 300 ml of the cooking water.

Sauce base: Heat the oven to 180°C / 350°F. In a wide pan, warm 80 ml of the olive oil over medium-low and cook the onion, carrot, and celery gently for 12–15 minutes until completely soft and sweet, not browned. Add the garlic for the last 2 minutes.

Stir in the tomato purée and paprika and fry 1 minute, then add the chopped tomatoes, oregano, and the reserved bean water. Simmer 25–30 minutes, until it darkens and thickens. Season generously now — salt, pepper, and the sugar if it tastes sharp.

Greens (optional): Wilt the chard or spinach in a dry pan or a splash of boiling water, then drain and squeeze it hard in a colander or a clean tea towel. Squeezing is the whole trick — unsqueezed greens release water into the dish and thin the sauce you just spent half an hour building. Chop roughly and set aside.

Combine: Fold the drained beans through the sauce along with another 30 ml of olive oil, and the squeezed greens if using. It should look slightly too loose, almost soupy — it will reduce a lot in the oven. Add more bean water if it doesn't.

Bake: Tip into a wide shallow baking dish so there's plenty of surface, drizzle the last 40 ml of olive oil over the top, and bake uncovered for 60–75 minutes. Don't stir. The sauce thickens and the exposed beans on top go brown and slightly chewy — those are the best ones.
Rest and finish: Leave 20 minutes out of the oven. Scatter over the dill, parsley, and mint if using, pour on the raw olive oil, and serve warm or at room temperature with lemon and bread.
tips: Quick version with tinned beans — no soak, no simmer, about 1 hr 10 min total instead of two and a half hours. Skip steps 1 and 2 entirely and start at step 3. Use 3 x 400 g tins of butter beans, drained and rinsed, and replace the reserved bean water with 200 ml water or vegetable stock. Fold them in gently at step 6 as they break more easily, and bake 40–45 minutes. The texture is softer and you lose some of the bite, but it is a genuinely good weeknight version.

The one rule that matters: beans must be completely tender before they meet the tomato. Acid halts softening, so a bean that goes into the sauce slightly firm stays slightly firm for the whole bake, no matter how long you give it.
Old dried beans never soften properly. If a batch refuses to cook after 90 minutes, it's the beans, not you — buy from somewhere with turnover.

The 150 ml of olive oil is not a typo. This is ladera — the oil emulsifies with the tomato and becomes the sauce. Cut it and you get watery beans in tomato juice, which is where most disappointing versions go wrong.

Adding the oil in three stages does more than pouring it all in at once: the first 80 ml carries the aromatics, the 30 ml with the beans coats them, and the last 40 ml on top fries the surface beans as it bakes.
Cook the onion and carrot far longer than feels necessary. That slow sweetness is the backbone; rushing it is the second most common failure.
Bake uncovered and don't stir. You want evaporation and a browned top, not a stew.
It is genuinely better on day two and best at room temperature, which is how it's usually eaten in Greece. Keeps 5 days, and the flavour deepens each one.
